subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: Hon. A. K. MACLEAN moved the second reading of Bill No. 35 to amend the Meat and Canned Foods Act.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I have already explained this Bill to the best of my ability, and I do not think the House should press me for further information until we are in

committee. The purpose of the Bill is to fix a standard can for the packing of lobsters, the sizes being 3, 6, 9, 12 and 16 ounces. The Bill will provide that when lobsters are sold in Canada they must have a label showing the exact contents of the can; that is, the dry lobster meat and not the gross weight of the contents. The law at present provides that a pound can shall contain 14 ounces and smaller cans are based upon that standard, so that we have 3i, 7J and 101 ounces. This is undesirable from the standpoint of the consumer. Those who are engaged in the packing of lobsters also object to it because it subjects them to the charge of possible fraudulent practices on the public.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
When the resolution
was introduced I noticed that the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) said that the weight was to be not printed on the label but stamped in the tin receptacle. I had no time to read this Bill and I do not know whether this provision is in it or not. That statement, coming from the chairman of the committee on fisheries, il took for granted to be so. Now I understand from the minister that there is no provision of that kind and there is nothing to show what the weight of the contents will be. There is a statement as to the quality or kind of shell fish contained in the tin but there is nothing on the label as to weight. Is that correct?

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Cans of lobster sold within Canada mlust contain a label showing the weight of lobster meat regardless of the liquid contained in the tins. If this Bill passes as it is and our lobsters are exported to the United States they will then conform with the American law which requires that the weight of the tin or can must be printed on the label. There is no provision as far as I know requiring that the weight be stamped on the can. I think the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (iMr. Fielding) was in error when he made that statement. I quite recollect his making the statement but at the time I was not sure whether he was right or wrong. I do not think there is any law requiring the weight to be stamped on the can. The great proportion of our lobsters are exported to Europe, largely to the English market, whence they go to various European countries. There is nothing in the British law requiring a label, or the statement of the weight on being imported into England, but when the cans are sold in England they must have a label and

the wholesale dealers attend to that in England. If English merchants sell these canned lobsters in France the labels must be in French and that is done in London. If they are sold in Belgium or Greece, the labels must be in tbe language of the country to which they are shipped. I think there is no way of avoiding that as our export lobsters reaching the London market are largely shipped to European countries.
Mr. MelSAAC: If I understand aright, the cans provided for in this Bill are such as have been hitherto used by lobster packers?

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. McI'SAAlC: I understand there is no change contemplated in the arrangement which existed prior to 1917. That is the desire of the packers in the province from which I come. They desire that no change shall be made and they favour the arrangement for putting three, six, nine and twelve ounces in the can. As to the other arrangement, they say that fourteen ounces of lobster meat cannot possibly be put into the cans they have. The cans they are now using have become standard, the manufacture of them goes right along and a change in the cans would involve a great amount of expense, new standard's and new machinery. If this carries out the arrangement which prevailed hitherto it is, I think, satisfactory to the packers all over the province of Prince Edward Island.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why does the minister depart from the usual weights of a pound, half pound and quarter pound?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I would remind the House that we are not in committee. The minister has already spoken. If, however, he should desire to answer the question it will be in order to do so.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I am only too anxious to give my hon. friend the information he desires, but if he is willing to allow us to go- into committee I shall endeavour to satisfy him.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: In past years the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr, Loggie) has been cited in the House as an authority on this very subject. I understand that he knows a great deal about canning and is interested in the canning business. The minister has made the statement that this Bill is acceptable to the great majority of canners. I, for one, for the purpose of information, would like to hear from the hon. member for Northumberland to know just how the canners look upon it.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to- be able to say that the proposals before the House are the findings of the packers, or a majority of them. In reply to a question by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie), I would say that the present law enacts that lobsters may be exported -without labels, and I understand this legislation does not in any way change that. What is done in this case is that when shell fish are imported into Canada for consumption a label must be put on the can indicating the net contents. But when Canadian lobsters are packed for export it	is not
necessary under the present law to have the tin stamped, although some packers do that for their own protection. As far as I understand the situation, it is the desire of the packers that the weights prescribed here be made the standard weights irrespective of what you call the can-each containing three, six, nine, twelve and sixteen ounces. These will be known as standard sized cans. I do not know whether or not the packers will make them known to -the trade as numbers three, six, nine, twelve and sixteen. I know I have no doubt that hon. gentlemen present are aware that a .No. 2 fruit can contains only about twenty ounces or a pound and a quarter. A gallon can is known to the trade as a No. 10, but it does not hold an Imperial gallon.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
It is very interesting to hear from the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) in regard to the views o.f the packers on this question. I have no doubt that the view he has expressed coincides exactly with the packers' views in regard to the packing of lobsters, .in which my hon. friend is deeply interested. I -am not very well informed in tegard to this matter, but it might toe interesting to the House if the minister (Mr. A. K. Maclean)-or if he cannot do so he might get somebody else to do it for him-would explain whether the partners in this business-I refer to the consuming public-have been considered and how they feel about the .question of reducing the weight of canned lobsters.
Bill read second time, and the House went into Committee on the Bill.
On section 1-"Dry lobster meat and dry meat."

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
It seems to me that "dry
lobster meat" is a misnomer; there is no such thing as dry lobster meat. Lobsters are put .in a can with pickle and then the
can is sealed, consequently, when the can is opened, the meat is not dry. It seems to me that the word "dry" should be left out of this section; it would be sufficient to say "lobster meat."

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
There probably
might be something to be said in favour of my hon. friend's suggestion, but it will do no harm to leave the clause as it is. The word "dry" is used in many other clauses of the Act, and if my hon. friend's suggestion is adopted it -will involve the amendment of other sections which are not in this Bill. No harm can be done by leaving the clause as it is. My hon. friend- may toe literally correct in saying that lobster meat is not dry, but it is necessary to give a definition of lobster meat after it is removed from the liquid contents of the can. In view of the effect it will have upon other clauses in the Act, I hope my hon. friend .will not -press his amendment at the present time.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I do not think the minister has sufficiently answered the point I raised. There are other fish to which this applies as well as lobsters. For instance, nobody can s.ay that mackerel put up in pickle in a barrel is dry fish. The minister ought to see that the language employed in the Bill is correct; there is no necessity for the term which is now to be found there. .Even if the amendment involves -changing other clauses let us do it and have the nomenclature right.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I must confirm what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Duff) has said in reference to "dry lobster meat." If -that term is insisted on it will create confusion in the minds of the people of the Maritime Provinces who are accustomed to regard "dry fish" as fish which -has undergone the process of being dried.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I cannot appreciate the point which my hon. friend makes. I do not think it at all relevant to this section of the Act, which applies to shell fish, and does not refer to fish dried by any other process in the Maritime Provinces or elsewhere. When the lobster is in cans it is contained in a liquid and in order to determine the weight of the lobster meat free of the liquid, the statute proposes to designate it as "dry lobster meat. When the liquid is drained from that -meat it, relatively speaking, is dry lobster meat. It is necessary to use a term which distinguishes between the lobster meat after it has been drained and taken from the liquid and

the lobster meat when it is in the can with the liquid-some term which is in contradistinction to the meat in the liquid. I do not see what better term there could be than the one used in the clause, and therefore it had better stand.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why not have the clause read that one minute after the can has been opened and the meat turned out that meat shall be drained? As the hon. member (Mr. Turgeon) says, there is a term in the fish trade which designates dry fish and another term which designates pickled fish. Dry fish means fish that has been sun-cured or cured by artificial means. The term " dry fish " must appear in other paragraphs of the Act.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It may appear in other clauses of the Act, but we are now dealing with a section which has reference to shell fish, which must be treated differently from other fish.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The ordinary person who
reads this clause where "dry lobster meat" is spoken of, and then notices that the term "dry fish" is used in other sections, will surely be greatly confused unless some change is made in the wording. If the word "dry" were omitted, leaving the designation as " lobster meat," it would cover the point.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-description of contents and minimum weight to be marked on cans.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Will the minister explain how the can is to be marked-whether it is the can itself or the label on the can?

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It surely is possible to leave out the word "dry" in the eighteenth line of this section and have it read, " the minimum weight in avoirdupois of the meat in the can plainly printed in a conspicuous manner."

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend's case was much stronger when, he was discussing the previous section .than it is now. I was about to point out to him that this clause discloses the fallacy in the argument he was making a moment ago.

The purpose of this clause is to the effect that the weight in avoirdupois of the contents of the can containing fish other than lobster shall be the weight of the contents of the can.
No liquid is added to salmon when it is canned, a little salt may be added, but an oily substance is exuded gradually from the fish, and therefore it would be unfair to say in the case of salmon and many other kinds of fish that the contents should be the exact weight of the fish meat. In the case of lobsters it is absolutely necessary to place in the can some preservative liquid, and the purpose of the legislation is to ensure that the weight expressed on the label shall be the weight of the lobster meat, not as in the can with the liquid, but as dried meat-that is, after opening the can and allowing the liquid to drain away for the space of one minute. For that reason we distinguish between lobster meat in and out of the preservative liquid, and in the latter case we call it dry meat and give it a statutory definition. Therefore, my hon. friend"s point is not so strong in this as in the other ease, and rather confirms the position I took when this Bill was before the House last week.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I cannot agree with the minister. It is quite evident that although he has lived in the fish country for a number of years he does not know the way fish are packed or he would not give the committee such information. It is a well known fact that when a fisherman packs fish he allows' a certain amount for the pickling

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I was not talking of the packing of all fish, but of certain kinds of fish.	[DOT]

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Certain kinds of fish are fish all the same.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Take the case of salmon. Probably I have seen as many packed as my hon. friend-and I suppose neither of us has seen any.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I have seen a few salmon packed in cans and in barrels. I do not pretend to know much about salmon, but I certainly know more than does the introducer of this Bill. The minister said that when salmon was packed a certain amount of oil exuded after a certain time. I was proceeding to say that there are other fish in the same position as salmon in that regard. The difference between my hon. friend and myself is that I know, and he does not know. For instance, when a

fisherman packs a barrel of mackerel, instead of packing 200 pounds he packs 205 pounds to allow for a certain amount of wafer or pickle. So my hon. friend's argument in relation to salmon is not a good one. He argued that this first clause could not -be changed because there were so many other clauses in the Act that would also have to be changed. Now he has taken another tack altogether in regard to the second clause.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No, it is my hon. friend who has taken another tack.

subtopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
What is the particular effect of the amendment in clause 2? From a hasty comparison of the amendment with the Act I see very little difference.
Mr. A. K. MAOLEAiN: The language of the Act might be construed as requiring that upon the label upon a can of fish, say salmon, the weight of the contents should he simply the weight of the fish, minus oil or other substance exuded from the fish while it was in the can. That was not considered fair by the department. Let me illustrate. For instance, in the case of a pound can of salmon over 16 ounces is put in as a matter of practice. If the salmon remains in the can a certain time a quantity of oil is exuded from the meat. This amendment will permit the weight of the oil so exuded to be comprised in the weight of the contents of the can. The oil is not lost; it can be used with the fish. subtopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY SYSTEM.

speechtext: The House resumed the adjourned debate on the motion of Hon. Mr. Reid for the second reading of Bill No. 33, respecting the acquisition by His Majesty of the Grand Trunk Railway system.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY SYSTEM.
subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
heard that great financial expert, the exMinister of Finance (Sir Thomas White)- *whom I respect as much as' does any other anember-say that' the financial condition -of Canada is serious, and that we are not in a position to assume further liabilities-mot even for .the payment of bonuses to our returned heroes, who to-day are clamouring for some assistance. But, Sir, if there is one form of exipenditure that we should endeavour to assume to-day it is whatever may be necessary to help our returned heroes who risked their lives for us on the bloody fields of Flanders and Belgium. No one need tell me that the soldier who spent many months under fire in the trenches, whether or not he may now seem to be as healthy as he was before, is in as good physical condition as he was before he enlisted. His nervous system has suffered more or less and he requires all the assistance and encouragement and opportunity that we can give to him.
The report of the board of arbitration as to the value of the shares of the Grand Trunk is to be final; the representatives of the people are to have no opportunity of passing judgment upon it. I contend that that report should be submitted to the people, through their representatives in Parliament, for consideration and decision. The day of rule by commissions and Orders in Council should now be passed; we should revert to democratic principles in the administration of our affairs.
It is said that the connection of the Grand Trunk with the Grand Trunk Pacific gives us the reason why the Grand Trunk is today in the condition that it is. It is my opinion that the Grand Trunk should be dealt with separately from the Grand Trunk Pacific. I admit that the position of the Grand Trunk Pacific is such that we have had to take it over; it has been put under receivership by the Government. Hon. gentlemen speak of receivership for the Grand Trunk as being a calamity, but they did not hesitate tb put the Grand Trunk Pacific under receivership. If it is practicable and desirable to have the Grand Trunk Pacific in receivership, I submit that it would be equally practicable and desirable to place the Grand Trunk, the parent company, in the hands of a receiver, as was the case with the Grand Trunk Pacific.
No doubt appeals will be made on behalf of the thousands of shareholders of the Grand Trunk, many of thein people of small means in England and on this continent, who bought the shares on the strength of -I will not say false representations, but

hasty representations, in many cases, to say the least, while the Grand Trunk were not looking after the interests of their road as they should have been. I shall always sympathize with holders of stock who were induced by exaggeration to enter into such speculation. But we must remember that our first sympathy is for the three or four hundred thousand returned men who fought our battles overseas and who need every possible assistance from us.
During the period from 1906 to 1916 $36,000,000 was paid by the company in dividends to the shareholders. Had they applied that amount to the improvement and maintenance of the road it would not be in the condition that- it is in to-day, and the company, instead of trying to load the railway on the country, would be refusing to part with it. My advice to the company is : Let your shareholders do without dividends for another ten years and during that time direct all your energies to the operation, maintenance and equipment of the road; put into it every dollar that you can raise, and after a while you will be able to commence paying dividends to the shareholders.
There is another reason why I am opposed to the taking over of the Grand Trunk Railway system to-day. If one speaks of the East, or of the West, or on behalf of any particular portion of the East or of the West, that does not mean that he looks at these matters from a narrow or sectional point of view. Our country is one of immense territory stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and naturally the conditions in its various parts are diversified; the products of the different sections vary. It is only by harmonizing the different elements of the country, facilitating the production and distribution of commodities throughout the whole country, taking full
5 p.m. advantage of the different strategical positions, so to speak, occupied by different portions of our land, that we can possibly adjust conditions satisfactorily and do what is best for the national good. One of the reasons, then, why I am opposed to. this project is that it is against the interests of the Maritime Provinces, more particularly against the interests of the ports of St. John and Halifax. I do not make this assertion from any provincial point of view. I believe, as I have already said, that the ports of St. John and Halifax have been placed where they are on the maritime coast of Canada by the hand of Providence for the well-being and prosperity of the whole of our country. In the words of George Etienne Cartier at the time of

Confederation, when he advocated the construction of the line of railways which would have for its purpose the linking together of these different parts of Canada, the presence of these ports on the maritime coast have a tendency to rid Canada of the necessity of being under the whim of the collectors of customs of the United 'States.
What reason is there to-day for the taking over of the Grand Trunk? The Transcontinental brings the products of the great Prairie Provinces from Winnipeg, the centre of the grain production of the West, by the shortest route to our national open ports, shortening the distance of carriage by four hundred miles. This line has not been given the fair trial that it should have been given by the Government since 1911; but notwithstanding that neglect it carried the grain of the West last year to the Maritime Provinces four cents a bushel cheaper than it was carried by any other railway. If that road had been given a fair chance we would not to-day be under the necessity of sending out the greater portion of our wheat through American channels.
It is said by some that we have too many railroads in Canada; that we do not need all these transcontinental lines.
We need these three transcontinentals. It may be that the present railway situation is due to different governments of Canada having refused to adopt the principle of the nationalization of railways simultaneously with the construction of the Intercolonial forty years ago. In consequence, the private railroads have all been looking for communication with the great centres of distribution, Saskatoon, Winnipeg,- Port Arthur, and so on, which has led to much duplication. Nationalization of the railways years ago would have avoided this duplication. It was in the interests of Canada that the Transcontinental railway should be built, because it brought the maritime ports four hundred miles nearer to Winnipeg.
There is another matter I wish to refer to in connection with this legislation. The ports of Halifax and St. John will be brought into competition with Portland, Maine. We have spent or are spending $40,000,000 on improving the port of Halifax, and $10,000,000 or $15,000,000 in improving the facilities at St. John. In passing I might say that one of the hon. members for Halifax stated when he was on this side of the House that the location of the facilities at Halifax was not the best. However, we are spending these great sums on these two maritime ports, and now we
propose to take away their trade and send it to Portland, Maine.

speechtext:
No, we must not send our wheat, our horses or our cattle to the United States where we can get a better price, but we are to give Boston, Portland and New York the advantage of our export trade. When the Liberal party had approved of the construction of the National Transcontinental from Winnipeg East, and of the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to the Pacific Coast, there was another proposal submitted to Parliament and the people of Canada, for securing the shipment of goods through Canadian ports, thereby building up the business of those ports and of our own railways. A resolution was passed by the Liberal administration in 1906 or 1907 by which importers of goods from Great Britain enjoyed the British preference only in case their importations came through Canadian ports. That was done, first, to develop greater trade with the British Empire, and secondly, to encourage the railroads we were building in Canada. To-day we * hear of public opinion in Ontario in favour of the nationalization of the railways, but for years men did not dlare mention that principle. It was also from Ontario that the resolution I have spoken of met with the greatest opposition, some two or three Ontario members on the Liberal side going so far as to vote against their leader and against the resolution. In view of such strong opposition to a measure of national interest, what opposition may we not expect to-day to a proposal to divert Canadian trade from our own ports to the ports of the United' States? The present outlet of the Grand Trunk is not one of our maritime ports, but Montreal, and thence to Portland. Now trade does not always follow the flag; it follows the streams that are open to it, and if you open the streams of trade from Montreal to Portland, as against Montreal to St. John and Halifax, trade will follow the stream and will be diverted to Portland. That applies not only to the roads west of Montreal, but to the roads east of Montreal. The money that has been spent on improving the ports of Halifax, St, John, and Quebec is apparently a secondary consideration with this Government.
When the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) was speaking the other day, my hon. friend from Royal (Mr. McLean) asked

as ito the possibility of trade being diverted from St. John to Portland. The minister's answer did not satisfy me, and I put the same question to him in a more concise form. I used as near, as I remember, the words. of the resolution of 1906 or 1907. I asked whether ocean traffic collected on the Grand Trunk west of Montreal and designated for ocean ports would continue to go to the ports of Halifax and St. John, and the minister replied that he could not add anything to the explanation he had given to my hon. friend from Royal. What was his answer to that hon, gentleman? He said:
Of course, when we are on the Bill, I shall be glad to discuss that matter, but I might say this evening that the ports of .St. John and Halifax have been and are being still further developed for our own Canadian ocean terminate, and the Government intend using those ports to their fullest capacity. There is no doubt about that. We have now the Transcontinental which. was originally built for that purpose right into St. John. But Portland is a portion of the Grand Trunk system and the hon. member will understand that a large portion of the Grand Trunk is In the United States. There is the Central Vermont and other portions of that line, so that Portland will have to be used to a certain extent for portions of the Gtjpnd Trunk railway system. But X want to impress upon the hon. member that there is no intention of not carrying out the policy of the Government in the past of developing and keeping our traffic in our own Canadian ports so far as it is possible to do that.
The maritime road was a masterpiece of railroad construction and was a credit to the entire Dominion. It was built for heavy transportation, having more particularly in view the shipment of western products to maritime ports with a minimum. of cost. But, I repeat, owing to a disastrous turn of events in 1911, there was a change of administration, with the inauguration of a policy which threatens to rob us of the full benefit of our national ports. The Minister of Railways, who' I regret is not present, tersely says: "You have the Transcontinental running from Moncton." The policy of the Government has been to bring all possible traffic from the prairies and from the West via Winnipeg, not to Quebec or Moncton, but to Cochrane, diverting it towards Toronto and giving it to the Grand Trunk, and sending it to the ports of New York, Boston and Portland. It is with considerable apprehension that I view this condition of affairs. Possibly, Mr. -Speaker, hon. members may think that I exaggerate, but let me assure my hon. friend, the member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) that there are others in the Mari-
[Mr. Turgeon.l
time Provinces who are equally as concerned as I am over the possibilities of the legislation now before the House. Only last Friday night the St. John Board of Trade passed a resolution in connection with the subject, expressing their opposition to the acquisition by the Government of the Grand Trunk railway in the absence of more reassuring information than they at present have. That resolution reads:
Resolved, that this council views with grave apprehension the acquirement by the Government of Canada of the Grand Trunk Railway, including that feature which would involve the owning and operating of a railway in a foreign country, and in the absence of fuller information would oppose the plan. The council would, however, welcome any person that the Government might feel disposed to depute to explain to the board the advantages to the country of the action proposed, and in the meantime would maintain an open mind on the subject.
A copy of this resolution was sent to the Government for their information. I regret that the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Wigmore) is not in the House. If he were I would ask him if he has not already been deputed to convey to the people whom he represents the views of the Government in regard to the railway situation. At the beginning of the session I drew the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that there was not a representative from New Brunswick in the Cabinet, and expressed the opinion that it was a matter of vital importance to that province that it should have such representation, at least to the extent of one member. Two months have passed since I made that representation, but no one from New Brunswick has been invited to join the Cabinet. And when I learned that this resolution would come before the House I thought that my hon. friend from St. John would be sent by the Government to pacify his constituents and give them every assurance that the interests of the country would not suffer as a result of this great undertaking which is contemplated by the Government. Let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the Board of Trade of St. John is by no means a political body, and certainly it is not Liberal in its sentiments. It is purely and simply a commercial organization, and the consensus of its influence tends, if anything, to the exclusion of Liberalism. When therefore that council in St. John appeals to the Parliament of Canada upon such a vastly important proposition as this, its representations, in my opinion, deserve every possible consideration. Now, the .Minister of Railways said the other day that he would give an explanation. Well, Sir, there are some

explanations that, strangely enough, do not explain anything, and we are yet to learn from the hon. minister that the commercial value of our own national ports will not in reality depreciate. We have been told that our national debt is so vast as to stagger the imagination and that it will tax our greatest ingenuity to make both ends meet. We are faced with a yearly expenditure on interest aggregating some $175,000,000; yet we are going to undertake, by the acquisition of the Grand Trunk, an enormous annual expenditure.
Now, I appeal to my western friends who have left the Government because of their disagreements with them in regard to tariff questions. The farmers of the West, as well as those of the East, have been expecting a reduction of the tariff from day to day, and from year to year, in order to be able to revive their activities in the further production of food npt only for our country but for the countries in Europe. They have claimed that they cannot produce to advantage because of the tariff exactions made upon them. They are clamouring for a reduction in tariff duties. They have been told by the Government to wait for another year or two. They were told last session to wait for the ministerial commission which would be appointed to travel over the country, take evidence and see what could be done in regard to the reduction of the tariff. The session ended the first week of July last, the summer is over but another session was called without regard to the work of this commission. We have been here for two months and the ministerial commission has not started out yet. We have been told to take as much time as we desired for the consideration of this question. We may be here if we -wish until November or December but in the meantime the tariff commission remains in Ottawa and the producers of the West will have to wait for another year. How does that situation agree with the demand for tariff reduction from the West? The farmers of the West have no interest in this railway. It is the people of Ontario who want to make further connections between the Grand Trunk and Winnipeg. They want another outlet to the West and they will have to get that outlet either through North Bay or Port Arthur.
The situation is serious. I know that the Grand Trunk Pacific has to be 'administered. 'in some way or other by the Government. Let us decide at once that we will take over the Grand Trunk Pacific, add it to the Transcontinental and have one national railway. In doing this we will
certainly add again to the debt of the country but the country is confronted with a situation, not with a principle. Let some means be devised by the Government so that they can come to an arrangement with the directors of the Grand Trunk to relieve them of their responsibilities in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Let us relieve them from these responsibilities and let the country assume them, take the road over and have one line from the Pacific to the Atlantic. Time will reveal that when the Grand Trunk Pacific was constructed it was constructed in the interests of the country. The requirements of the country demanded it and if the policy in regard to it had been maintained, if we had refused to duplicate that line from Edmonton to the Pacific coast by aiding the Canadian Northern to the extent of 800 miles we would not be confronted with the position that we face to-day. I think this is the best possible solution of the situation. Let some means be devised by which some arrangement would be made to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific and tell the directors of the Grand Trunk that they will have to exercise economy, raise means in all available ways, stop paying dividends to the shareholders that are not earned, and put every; dollar of receipts into the maintenance and improvement of their road.
This project, since its introduction a few days ago, has been receiving the earnest consideration of thinking people throughout Canada. As we have seen by the resolution passed by the Board of Trade of St. John, and expressions coming from other directions, the people of Canada are considering the situation and are averse to putting any further financial burden upon the country. There are others who do not partake of the views of the Government but who are offering the Government every possible assistance in taking over the Grand Trunk Pacific and stopping at that in order not to plunge the country into a more serious financial condition than that in which it finds itself to-day. If we go on a few steps farther we may find the situation not only dangerous but disastrous.
My attention has been called to a letter published in the Ottawa Citizen the other day from one whom I consider an authority upon the resources of the country and the way in which they should be developed. In his earnest devotion to Canada he takes second place to none. The fact that he is a Liberal does not mean that he is not a Canadian. His suggestions merit the attention of the Canadian people and more particularly of those who are conversant

with his activity, his energy, his success in life and his devotion to his country. I refer to the Hon. Senator Edwards, of Ottawa, who to-day, unfortunately, is not permitted to come to the Senate and explain his views, and suggestions, patriotic as they are and worthy of the commendation of the Canadian people. He expresses my views not only upon the question of the nationalization of railways, but the position of the country and the future of our resources, resources which are immense, but which may be wasted as they have been in some directions in the United States, where they have exhausted their timber resources and to-day have to come to Canada for their supplies. If we pay no more attention to our resources than the Americans have done we will in the future regret the unwise freedom which we have taken in their development without consideration of the future needs of the country. After explaining his views, Senator Edwards arrives at certain conclusions. LeLme read his words so that there will be no misapprehension:
No one should criticise to any extent without offering some alternative to that which is suggested. As I understand, it is the purpose of the Government to take over the old Grand Trunk Railway system and add it to the many miles of existing railway which are already under the administration of the Government of Canada. Now, so far as I am concerned, I see no justification whatever for taking over the Grand Trunk Railway proper. It is a railway having a great portion of its trackage in the United States. It was constructed and is owned by British capital. It is true that the affairs of that railway are complicated by reason of its having undertaken responsibility with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific. In my judgment the Government should not go beyond making arrangements to relieve the Grand Trunk system of that responsibility. That done, the old Grand Trunk system would be in its former position.
This is what I claim should be done. Let the Government make the best possible arrangement as to the Grand- Trunk Pacific, from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast. Let them secure a good transcontinental railway, under Government ownership and control, and then allow the Grand Trunk themselves to do the best they possibly can, and direct their energies into the improvement of their road, and in time they will be able to surmount the difficulties which confront them without forcing Canada into a state which approaches a dangerous crisis, not to say any more. Our resources are well known in England. Let the directors and- the shareholders of the Grand Trunk place before the capitalists of England the value of those

resources and the necessity for extending temporary assistance. That assistance will then be obtained from the . capitalists of England and also from the capitalists of the United States, where the Grand Trunk likewise operates. In the general interests of Canada I cannot support the Bill now before the House. I cannot support the project for taking over the -Grand Trunk, because I see no national necessity for it. If it is not ar national necessity it must consequently be against the interests of the Maritime Provinces; and it is opposed to the very idea of Confederation which brought together the Canadian East and the Canadian West, and had for its object freedom of trade throughout Canada under every possible circumstances which could have been foreseen fifty years ago. To-day we live on peaceful terms with the United States, and I hope that condition of peace will continue for centuries to come. The United States will undoubtedly do everything possible for the improvement of their own railroads and the development of their trade and their wealth, regardless of the needs of any other country. We also have our own interests to guard, and I fo-re-' see the danger in this project of a diversion of Canadian trade to United States seaports. For that reason I regard this policy as not only opposed to- the best interests of the Maritime Provinces but highly prejudicial to Canada as a whole. If Canada as a whole is not prosperous, happy, and contented how can any portion of the Dominion be in that desirable state. It might be an advantage to Toronto to centralize the traffic and the offices of a great railway in that city, but that would not necessarily be in the national interests, Toronto does not constitute the whole of Canada. I have every possible respect for Toronto and the press but when that press make representations that are of a deceptive character, we must call upon the people outside of Toronto, and even outside of Ontario, to see that Canadian interests shall be preserved for the East as well as for the West, and that we shall embark upon no policy that will mar the prospect of having a happy, contented, and prosperous nation. For .the reasons I have given. I shall vote against the Government's project.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY SYSTEM.
subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The
question that is under review by the House at the present time is unquestionably, one of the most important-if not the most important-that has come before this Parliament. It is important for several reasons. It is important because it means the incurrence, of a very considerable addition to

the public obligations of the country. It is important also, because if this legislation is passed, one of the oldest railroads in Canada shall disappear. Now in any consideration of the question we have, I think, from the very force of circumstances, to take into account what the position of the Grand Trunk is at the present time. It is a matter of certainty that to-day the Grand Trunk railway is in a very difficult-and in reality when one surveys all the circumstances of the case-an almost, if not quite hopeless position. This is due to the obligations incurred by it in the building of the Grand Grand Trunk Pacific in order that it might have a through line to the prairies of the West and an outlet to the Pacific ocean. An argument has been put forth by the directorate and management of the Grand Trunk that it should be relieved of any liability in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific. In the face of all the circumstances I think it is impossible for this Parliament to concede that position for a moment

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY SYSTEM.
subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
-and the best evidence of this is found in the report of the Royal Commission on Transportation that was appointed a few years ago to investigate the whole railway situation of the Dominion. What is the judgment of this commission in respect to that particular point? Let me illustrate by reading a brief excerpt from the report of the commission. This is taken from a letter which was sent by Mr. W. H. Biggar, K.C., General Counsel for the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific railway. In that letter Mr. Biggar states:
The construction by the Grand Trunk interests of a line into the western provinces appears to have been first suggested by Mr. Hays to the late Sir Charles Rivers Wilson, then -President of the Grand Trunk, early in 1902. The correspondence between these two officials clearly shows that the chief purpose was the construction of a line to connect the Ontario dines of the Grand Trunk with the western provinces. The general outline of the scheme having received the approval of the directors of the Grand Trunk in London, Mr. Hays, on October 23rd, 1902, submitted it to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Prime Minister.
This is the statement of the General Counsel of the Grand Trunk railway, and I think clearly establishes the fact that the idea of building this transcontinental line originated in the minds of those who were then associated with the management of the old Grand Trunk railway. And of course, Mr. Speaker, for very natural reasons. The Grand trunk lines were confined to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec so far as
Canadian mileage was concerned. The management realized it was handicapped in operating a road within this circumscribed area, and that if the road was to reach a position of strength in the country it was necessary to reach out into the western provinces and get, as it developed, a portion of the profitable business that originated in that portion of the Dominion. Consequently, for very good reasons, they approached the Government of the day with the proposal that- this road should be built.
Now, in face of that how can we consider for one moment that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall be relieved of its liabilities in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific? I dismiss its responsibility for the operation of the National Transcontinental for the reason that the Government a few years ago, when that matter was under consideration, according to the Royal Commission I have referred to, practically relieved the Grand Trunk of any obligation to operate this portion of the system. But when we come to consider the position of the Grand Trunk in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific, we find, according to the statements of this same Royal Commission that. investigated our railway situation, that its present liabilities in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific reach $5,000,000 a year, and at the end of 1923 will reach $7,000,000 a year.

subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is under a misapprehension. The Grand Trunk was not under any obligation to operate the Transcontinental; it was the Grand Trunk Pacific that was under that obligation.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY SYSTEM.
subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
It was a slip of the tongue; I meant the Grand Trunk Pacific but in any event it amounts to the same thing. The existing obligations of the Government in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific amount, according to the statement of the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), a ferw days ago to probably $145,000,000. We have therefore in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific this situation: that the old Grand Trunk, through its guarantees, is liable for the interest on the moneys invested in that road to the extent of over $100,000,000, and the Canadian Government is interested to the extent of over $140,000,000. The information placed before the House a few days ago in respect to the position of the old Grand Trunk indicates clearly that it is an impossible position as far as the payment of the interest on its investment in the Grand Trunk Pacific

is concerned. I will admit that the last two years of railroad operation in Canada have been difficult years, and that it is perhaps unfair to take those as a true index of the business of the Grand Trunk; but even if we take the history of the Grand Trunk back for the last 15 years, we shall find that it has not at any time earned sufficient net revenues to meet its obligations on the Grand Trunk Pacific in addition to its own fixed obligations. Consequently I think we are perfectly safe in arriving at the conclusion that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is in the position where it cannot meet its obligations on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific. In fact, it requires no argument to demonstrate that fact, because it has been admitted by the Grand Trunk Tailway itself.
Now, what is the position of Parliament and the.country in respect to this? It seems to me there are only three courses open to us. First, to relieve the Grand Trunk -of its obligations in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and leave it as it was before this enterprise was undertaken. That, Mr. *Speaker, let me say, is a condition that- in my judgment will not be tolerated for a moment by the Canadian people. I do not think, in view of the fact of the part that the Grand Trunk Railway Company played in the initiation of this enterprise, that it should be relieved of its responsibility in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific. What, then, is the next course? It is for the Grand Trunk to go into liquidation. There are several reasons why that is not desirable. In the first place, it might seriously damage the financial credit of Canada. We must bear in mind that our country is a developing country, and that for many years we shall have to go *outside for assistance to finance our public enterprises. We have a large country with a population of only 8,000,000, but we hope that in 15 or 20 years we shall have a population of at least 15,000,000, and in order to carry on our national development it is necessary that Canada's credit be maintained unimpaired in the markets of the world. And in any case it is perhaps doubtful what would be the outcome of liquidation proceedings so far as the responsibility of the Dominion is concerned. It is doubtful, in my mind at any rate, whether it would relieve us entirely of our liability in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific. What, then, is the other course to be pursued? To my mind it is the course that the Government have proposed in this resolution which we are now considering, and which commends itself to my judgment as CMr. Crerar.]
the best way out of an extremely difficult situation.
We are not now discussing, Mr. Speaker, the question of whether this country should or should not commit itself to the principle of public ownership of railways. That question has been settled for us-settled, if you like, by the very force of circumstances that have developed in the last few years. We own to-day, independently of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, some 15,000 miles of railway mileage, and we are operating that mileage to-day-operating, it is true, through a company, but nevertheless the people of Canada in fact own and operate these roads. It is not a question, then, of the practicability of Government ownership. It' is, in my judgment, a matter of making the best of a bad situation.
What is the position of our Government railways? We have the Intercolonial, the oldest Government line in Canada, running from the Maritime Provinces, to the city of Montreal; then we have the Canadian Northern lines, the National Transcontinental, and the Grand Trunk Pacific. But a study of the situation reveals this fact, that'we have two Transcontinental lines, with a large number of branch lines in Western Canada-and I may say, those are located through the best territory in the West-with comparatively little branch mileage in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Now, if we are going to operate to the best advantage the existing mileage that the country possesses, is it not necessary from a sound business point of view to get additional mileage in the province of Ontario and also in the province of Quebec?
When the National Transcontinental was undertaken at the requestor at any rate, at the suggestion-of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, one of the arguments advanced in favour of it was that it would be a complementary system to the old Grand Trunk in Ontario; that the Grand Trunk required these extensions into the Western Provinces, required the transcontinental line, in order that they might more effectively carry on their business. If that argument was sound then-and it was considered sound-is it not equally true to-day that the Canadian people, having the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental, finds it necessary to 'have the old Grand Trunk as complementary to these systems? I think the question is beyond argument from a practical business point of view.
Some objections have been raised, particularly in a portion of the public press

of Canada, to the principle of public ownership. While I recognize that the question has much opposition, I say frankly, Sir, that I believe in the principle of public ownership, and there are strong evidences throughout the world that all democratic peoples are coming to a belief in it, But one of the strongest arguments advanced outside of this House against the public ownership of' railways in Canada is that it cannot be made to pay, and the experience of the Intercolonial is cited as evidence of this. I have taken the trouble to make some inquiry into the relative rates of the Intercolonial and Canadian Pacific railways in the past. In the year 1918- my authority for these figures is Mr. Payne, statistician of the Railway Department- the average freight rate on the Canadian Pacific railway was eighteen per cent higher than it was on the Intercolonial, and the average passenger rate was twenty-four per cent higher. I venture the assertion that if the Intercolonial had enjoyed during the past thirty years a parity of rates with those of the Canadian Pacific, we would not have had the deficits that have occurred in connection with the operation of that road.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY SYSTEM.
subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
When the House rose at six o'clock I was discussing the experience1 Canada has had with the Intercolonial railway and had referred to the arguments advanced against public ownership based on our experience with the Intercolonial as a road that had not been profitable. I pointed out that had freight ratps on the Intercolonial during the year 1918 been similar to those enjoyed by the Canadian Pacific railway probably an altogether different result would have been obtained. There is, however, this fact to be borne in mind, that the Intercolonial was not built- with the expectation of its being a paying railway. It, was part of the bargain of Confederation, and when one bears in mind that the Intercolonial has had to compete with cheap water rates during the whole of its career it is not much to be wondered at that deficits have occurred on the road. I submit that it is not fair to -cite the Intercolonial's failure to earn profits as evidence of a lack of virtue in the principle of public ownership.
There is another factor in connection with the Intercolonial that we may as well consider. There is no doubt that during its whole history the Intercolonial, up until very recent years at any rate, has been the subject of political management to a very great degree. I adduce these facts in support of my contention that the Intercolonial was never at any time considered seriously as a going business concern. The experience of Great Britain and the United States during the past few years has also been cited as evidence against the virtue of public ownership and the possibility of making public-owned roads pay. That also is not quite fair.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY SYSTEM.
subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Are we not now discussing this matter because private ownership has failed?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY SYSTEM.
subsubtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
We are. In the case of Great Britain and the United States the public operation of railways has been carried on under conditions of extreme stress during the war period, when operating costs were high, and when the full advantage of systematic operation could not be had; but even in Great Britain such a competent authority as Sidney Webb, who is an economist of repute in the United Kingdom, argues, and I think with considerable force, that government operation of railways there during the past few years has not been a financial failure, -and that if everything is fairly and evenly balanced up the railways of Great Britain under government operation have returned a very fair profit. I think it will be admitted by close observers that public operation in the United States during the years of the war has not had a fair trial. Those who argue that public ownership does not pay must surely have overlooked the experience of the railways of the United States during the past decade or more. I find on inquiry that on June 30, 1915, the latest figures I have, although I believe later ones have been published, there were 23,800 miles of railway in the United States exclusive of terminal and switching companies that were in receivership, embracing over 85 carriers. So it is not fair to argue that public ownership does not pay when we have striking evidence of private ownership failing to pay in a country like the United States. But what is the result of private railways going into receiverships in the United States? It is to create a public opinion through the newspapers and every possible public agency that- is available in support of a demand for increased rates in order that

private companies who have increased their capitalization through stock jobbing and other processes of that kind might earn dividends on an inflated capital value.
We can oite some evidence of public ownership in the Dominion of Canada to show that public ownership can pay its way. and I should like to direct the attention of the House briefly to the experience of the city of Winnipeg in the development of its city light and power. Ten years ago the citizens of Winnipeg were paying to a corporation controlled by Mackenzie and Mann ten cents per kilowatt hour for electric light, and a proportionate charge for electric power to drive the wheels of industry in that city. Efforts were made to get this privately-owned corporation to give 1be people a fair deal in the price of electric light and power, but without success, and a. very strong demand developed among the citizens that the city should under:ake the development of its own hydro electric system and the sale of light and power to the citizens at a lower rate than they were then paying. That proposal met with opposition, and with the same kind of opposition that public ownership of railways is meeting in Canada to-day. Financial authorities throughout the country argued that the city in undertaking this expenditure of millions of dollars was committing financial suicide, and that nothing but bankruptcy could eventually result. Nevertheless, when the by-law was submitted to the people it carried by a large majority and the project was undertaken. What has been the result? That enterprise to-day has invested in it more than $7,500,000, which all will agree is a considerable amount for a city of 200,000 people. During the last six years it has returned a profit of over $430,000, after caring for all proper charges in the way of depreciation and maintenance. This was fully established by an independent audit of the books of the city in respect to its light and power. But what else happened? The moment the city turned the switches on to deliver light and power to the city of Winnipeg it reduced the rate from ten cents to three and one-third cents per kilowatt per hour. The people of that city have for the last six or seven years enjoyed that reduced rate, and there has been a revenue, after caring for all charges, as I have ' just stated, of over $430,000. We have also the case, on a much larger scale, of the hydro-electric in Ontario.

I did not mention that fact because I am anxious to get through as quickly as possible. I know that there is a keen desire on the part of hon. gentlemen to get out in order to learn the election returns,' and I am indeed grateful to them for giving me an opportunity to conclude my remarks, since I am 'obliged to leave shortly to catch a train. Of course, the private corporation that previous to that time had been selling light and power at a much higher rate immediately made a reduction to meet the reduced rate of the city.
I am aware that there has been considerable criticism directed against the hydro-electric in Ontario, and I know that supposedly competent financial authorities have criticised the administration of that enterprise, and have stated that it imposes immense financial burdens upon the people of that province. But, Sir, there is no danger of imposing financial burdens upon a province like Ontario in a matter of this kind, if in the sale of the article produced, sufficient revenue accrues to meet interest on investment and provide a sinking fund to retire at their maturity the bonds 'by which the money is raised. And from what information I can get, that- is .precisely the situation in Ontario. Let us consider the advantage it has been to that province in the matter of cheap light and power, and the advantage it has proved to the rural parts of Ontario. I have discussed this matter with many farmers , of Ontario and they tell me that the introduction of hydro-electric into their municipalities and the consequent sale of electric energy on the farms is very largely changing the character of their agricultural work on the farms. Whereas hitherto the farmer's wife had to drive by hand a washing machine or chum and the other equipment in a farm house, this work is now done by electrical energy and the labour on the farm is correspondingly reduced. This is all accomplished after such provisions have been made as to make the enterprise pay its own way at every step of the journey.
The cases of the city of Winnipeg and of the Hydro in Ontario illustrate a fundamental difference between private ownership and public ownership in the operation of those utilities that are in their very nature natural monopolies. Private ownership is based on the principle of gain; it is an investment for profit. I do not find any fault

in proper limitations with that principle, which is perfectly laudable. On the other hand, public ownership is based on the idea of service at cost to the people, and I submit that in the case of great natural monopolies, such as railway transportation or the development of electrical energy, where by the very nature of the thing an individual or small group of individuals cannot carry on the service for themselves, it is in the interests of the State and of its citizens that the principle of public ownership should apply.
Another argument advanced against public ownership and operation of our railways is that it will provide a tremendous leverage to any political party in power to retain itself in office; that through the agency of your public railways an engine will be created whereby an existing party can maintain itself in power irrespective of the popular will. I do not know that public ownership offers any more danger in that respect than what we have suffered from under private ownership of our railways in this country, I think that all impartial students of the history of Canada for the last forty years will come to the conclusion that there has been no more potent influence operating in the public life of the country, operating on the legislation that flows from governments, than our private railway companies. We know the conditions that existed at the time of the Canadian Pacific railway forty years ago. I do not wish to criticise the legislators of those days. We know that the Canadian Pacific railway is a great railway and one that is well managed, but it is well to bear in mind that the people of [DOT]Canada have been very good to that railway, which has secured altogether in cash subsidies from the provinces and municipalities and governing bodies of Canada over $70,000,000, besides some 26,000,000 acres of rich and valuable land, and also, in British Columbia, some $38,000,000 worth of [DOT] completed road. Altogether, if you calculate in actual dollars and cents to-day what the Canadian Pacific railway has secured from the country, you will find that the total does not fall far short of $300,000,-[DOT]000 or $325,000,000.
