That would depend, of
[DOT]course, on the value placed upon the lands,
but I wish to be conservative in my estimates. Here is another aspect of the question :	Suppose the Canadian people had
built the Canadian Pacific railway; suppose it had not been built by private enterprise. We could have lost some ten or twelve million dollars a year during the whole period of its operation, and so far as the balance sheet of the country is concerned we would not be further behind than we are at the present time. Take the Canadian Northern railway. We all know what a bad influence it exercised on the public life of the country. We know how it lobbied in the Parlia^ ments of Canada, and in some of the provincial legislatures as (well, where it wished to extend its lines and get railway bonuses and guarantees and land grants. I know that I am on safe ground when I say that there has been no more unfortunate influence at work in the public life of the country than that of our private railway companies.
In considering this question, I would offer this suggestion to the Government, that in drawing up the agreement with the Grand Trunk railway upon which arbitration proceedings are to be based, they should be exceedingly careful to guard the public interest in every way. This is absolutely essential. The people of the country demand it and will hold the Government to strict account if it fails in this. For instance, the Grand Trunk should not be permitted to advance as an argument in the arbitration proceedings the plea that other railways were built that detracted from its business; nor, in my judgment, should its value be based on the existing values of equipment, buildings, rolling stock and all the other paraphernalia that goes into the operation of a railway. We know that the cost to-day of locomotives, cars, buildings, is almost double what it was prior to the war.
These conditions are not going to continue in this country; it may be four, five, or eight years, but eventually we will get back to something like pre-war conditions in reference to the cost of materials necessary to construct a railway and the equipment necessary to maintain it.
What will the position of the country be if we get this mileage? We will be, as some one said in the debate a few days ago, probably the largest owners of railway mileage on the continent of North America. I believe the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) estimated that we would have something like 21,000 or 22,000 miles of railway, if Parliament approves of the proposal of

natural resources. When the Government is carrying on its immigration policy I would suggest that it direct these immigrants as far as possible to lands adjacent to our own railways, with a view of building up business for those railways in the future. We have the lands and if we can get people to settle along our national railways will be creating a potential business for these roads in the future that will help to get us out of the difficulties that we have to surmount. There is good reason for hoping that a system of national railways can be made a great influence as a unifying power throughout Canada. Reference is frequently made to the character of our country, to its scattered population, the difficulty that exists, for example, in the people of the western provinces understanding the hopes and aspirations of the people of the Maritime Provinces and of Quebec. The same is true of the western provinces and of Ontario. Unfortunately, we have not a free interchange of newspapers between these portions of the Dominion. May we not entertain the hope that by means of this system of national railways we can create a national spirit of public pride in them' that will have a unifying effect among our people and give them something to be proud of from one end of *Canada to the other. It is not an impossibility-it is, in fact, a very possible and practical thing.
I do not wish to detain the House any longer, but I would add this: Canada is facing great burdens and the railway situation is admittedly a difficult one. The course that is being taken, while it, perhaps, affords much room for criticism, is, on the whole, the best course that we can follow. When we have our lines completed it will then be for the Canadian people, and for their representatives in Parliament, and for the Government who are entrusted with the administration of the country's laws, to use every legitimate means in their power to make it a success. I believe we can make it a success. I believe we can hand down to posterity an example and a tradition in this respect that will be worthy of the country .and worthy of the sacrifices Canada has made in the last four or five years.
Mr. PIERRE F. CASGRAIN (Charlevoix-Montmorency): Mr. Speaker, in 1911 the *Government that immediately preceded the present administration cherished the ambition to do better than the Laurier ministry. At that time the press of the country heralded the new Administration as a saviour which would keep Canada faithful to the flag and make the country prosper-

ous. The incoming ministry were pronounced a new broom that would sweep clean; sweep away all that- was bad in the previous administration of public affairs, and do better than their predecessors. But what happened? In 1911, when the Borden Government assumed office, our national debt was in the neighbourhood of $100,000,000. Six years afterwards it had mounted to about $336,000,000, and at present it approximates $2,000,000,000. It is true that the war largely increased our public debt and for the addition attributable to that cause there is perhaps not much criticism to be offered. Nevertheless, we notice that although the Government who were returned in 1911 constantly preached economy have overmanned all the departments of the Government- and increased by over 15,000 the number of civil employees, notwithsitanding their denunciation of the Laurier administration on the very same ground. As to railway matters, when the Borden Government assumed office they blamed the Laurier Administration for the existing railway situation and yet what do we find them doing? After assuming office in 1911 they continued the very same path that the preceding administration had been following.
That is to say, subsidies were lavishly granted to different railway companies, moneys advanced to them, and flheir bonds guaranteed in different ways. We saw the Canadian Northern people asking favours of the Government just as before, and finally forcing upon the Government the famous deal of 1917; and a year after we saw the stock of that company, which was declared valueless by the Drayton-Acworth Commission, valued by a board of arbitrators at about $10,000,000. This Canadian Northern railway, coupled with the other railways of the Government, according to a recent answer laid before the House in answer to a question put by an hon. member, had a deficit last year of about $9,041,464.62. The Canadian National railways to-day have a total interest paying debt of $460,225,148.93, and the amount of interest payable annually on this debt is $19,073,387.08. In view of this vast national indebtedness settled upon the country by different Administrations, and especially by the consummation of the Canadian Northern deal, is it wise to take another step towards completion of the nationalization of all our railways as now proposed? I say no, Mr. Speaker. The Government would be wise to " stop, look, listen.'
Let us see what certain authorities on railway problems have to say on the sub-

jeet. Mr. E. W. Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific railway, recently stated;
I am not attempting to persuade you to my views, they are not unalterable, but I am not convinced of the expediency nor wisdom of any such policy, because none of the advocates have been able to show ground for the faith that is in them, and before we change from a system which we understand, and which in the case of some companies at least has worked to the distinct advantage of Canada, we should be very sure that an improvement will be made and the results to the people, the owners, such as to warrant the extraordinary obligations they would assume.
It would be a pity, Mr. Speaker, to change, from 'a system we know to a system of which we know very little. The ex-president of the Canadian Pacific railway, Lord Shaugh-nessy, made this statement not very long ago:
We shall within a short period learn the experience of our neighbours to the south of us in the management of railways in that country, and we may have some exiperience of our own in that regard. I do not wish to have it understood that I am taking a stand opposed to the nationalization of railways. If the people of this country want it, and if the Government decide that the people want it, this Is a democratic country and they must have it. But whenever we start out upon that avenue, we should be very, very sure of our footing, or we may have a serious problem.
Before I go any further, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw your attention to those words:	,
If the people of this country want it, and it the Government decide that the people of this country want it.
The election of 1911, if I am not mistaken, was fought on the Navy and Reciprocity issues; there was no question of the nationalization of railways. The election of 1917 was fought on the Win-the-War policy, and nothing else; there was no question then raised as to the practicability of Government ownership. I am not aware that this Government holds any mandate to impose such a policy upon this country. Let us see, for example, what was done. In 1904, when the Laurier Administration proposed a new policy in the way of railway construction, and wanted to launch the famous Grand Trunk Pacific agreement, which is now so much criticised, they went to the people on that very issue, and as a result , of the election that policy was sanctioned by a majority of the electors. In 1911 the same administration wanted to go a step further and give to this country reciprocity with the United States. The same procedure was followed, and the result of that election is that to-day we have
the present Government administrating the affairs of the country. Surely, Mr. Speaker, it cannot be said that the present policy is . as democratic as the policy of the Laurier Administration. But there is one thing we may be sure of, that whether the people have decided that they want nationalization of railways, certainly the Government want it and has decided that the people want it, and we are going to have it at all costs.
Let us see what another authority said on the subject on the nationalization of railways. Sir William Hoy, general manager of South African railways and harbours, stated:
The wide conflict of practical evidence renders it extremely difficult to decide as to the relative advantages and disadvantages of State and private railways. On the whole, it would seem that the problem is one to ibe determined according to the geographical position and industrial, economic, political and social conditions of the country concerned, rather than according to the merits claimed for either system in other countries. The success or otherwise of State railways is influenced largely by the extent to which the management is freed from political influence. It is thus manifest that the problem is governed by many elements other than the purely economic.
Mr. Speaker, experience shows that politics always do creep into State management, irrespective of the statutory or other safeguards applied thereto, as in the case of Australia and Italy, and that the only managements immune from interference are the autocratic governments of Germany and Austria. The experience of England, France, Italy, and lately that of our neighbours, the United States, should suffice to convince us of the value of Government ownership. That is so true that President Wilson recently, upon his return from Europe after attending the Peace Conference, advocated that the railways which had been taken over and operated during the war under government control, should be handed back to their original owners. We find also that the United States Congress is taking action to avoid the injustice of the government operating railways in competition with privately owned railways; while here we find our own Government planning to build up a great railway system for the avowed purpose of attacking a privately owned railway which, every one will admit, has since its inception been giving most excellent service to the country and"is well able to continue doing so.
Is there anything more dangerous and more serious than this tendency to use government powers for the purpose of attacking



and injuring private industry? In certain quarters, especially in the western provinces, this policy is finding much favour. The protection of the vested rights was always one of the first principles of Anglo-Saxon legislation. Are we going to embark upon a policy of confiscation?-because, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion that is what this project amounts to. If this policy is followed opt as the Government propose it, there is reason to believe that sooner or later, due to the fact that the railway rates will have to be decreased because of competition with the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Pacific itself will have to be absorbed and come also within the Canadian National Railway system. I am afraid that that may happen if this project is carried out. I do not say that it will happen, but it is a possibility-so many strange things have been done during the last few years that that is quite liable to happen.
The complications which will result from the increase in the expenditures of the Government if this project is carried out places its acceptance beyond the limits of reason; because it is evident that should the Government operate all these railroads, especially the Canadian Pacific, they would not be able to attain anything like the standard of service which this company is now giving to the people of Canada or obtain a revenue which would enable them to pay anything like the dividend which the Canadian Pacific is paying at present to its shareholders.
Experience has taught us that under government control, and partly because of it, the cost of operating railways and telegraphs increases heavily and that in regard to the former there is a reduction in the service offered to the public. The public pays more heavily for what it gets, and very often what it gets is not up to the standard.
In glancing over the report of the' Dray-ton-Acworth Commission I find that it makes the following observation with regard to the Canadian Pacific:
There was given to the Canadian Pacific at the outset direct aid with a generous hand and the aid was continued up to the point when
the company could stand alone	The
people of Canada, in our view, have had good value for their money.
In my opinion the same should have been done with the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk as was done with the Canadian Pacific. The only thing these companies want is to be left alone that they may pursue their own course; let them work out their own salvation. If

they cannot do it now, in a few years they will be able to make both ends meet and to pay to their shareholders the amounts to which they are entitled having regard to the capital invested. But the Government, under the pretense of needing this company's railways to complete its system, wants to get control of the Grand Trunk in order, it is said-of course, we have no proof-to promote the interests of a certain faction which is back of the Government.
Let us see what, certain newspapers which are friendly to the Government have to say in reference to the matter. In the Ga-. zette of December 2nd last, editorial reference was made to a certain article which appeared in the Globe on a previous occasion. The Globe had stated very frankly and openly its opinion regarding this deal, as follows :
Canadian speculators, led by a former minister of the Crown, who had a good deal to do with the formation of the Union Government, are seeking to obtain control of large blocks of the common and preference stocks of the Grand Trunk railway in the belief that should the Government determine to take over the railway the value of these stocks will be greatly enhanced and a handsome profit will result from their forethought. A more sinister version of the same story, which may be no more than a slanderous invention, is to the effect that the group of men engaged in the alleged speculation are powerful enough to sway the decision of the Government, and are, therefore, not gambling on a possibility, but investing in a " sure thing."
That is the article that was published in the Gazette of that day, and both the Gazette and the Globe are, or were at that time, friendly to the Government; in fact, they helped to put the Government where it is to-day.
Last spring, if I mistake not, the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario was on. the job, urging the Government to take over the Grand Trunk Railway system. If I remember correctly the reports in the press at that time, Sir Adam Beck came to Ottawa and tried to force upon the leader of the Government the policy of the Hydro Electric Commission. But apparently the leader of the Government, Sir Robert Borden, took a strong stand in the matter and did not accede to the suggestion. Nobody thought at that time that the people who were promoting this deal would succeed.
We have another authority on this subject, a man who used to be a minister of the Crown and who expressed himself as entirely opposed to the policy which the Government is following to-day. I refer to the former Minister of Public Works, Hon. F. B. Carvell. He said:

Possibly the present Government may succeed where others have failed, but It is a lamentable fact that Government operation of railways has been one of the most tragic farces in this country that we have ever seen.
Sir Henry Drayton, who, I am told, is Minister of Finance-the newspapers now report that he has been elected-says in the Dray ton-Acworth report:
In our judgment it is not in the interests ot Canada that the operation of its railways should be in the hands of the Government. We know no country in the world where a democratic State owns and operates its railways, and the railways have not had an injurious influence on politics.
Another expert in political economy, one of our foremost economists, Professor Mavor, has said-and I would like my hon. friend (Mr. Crerar) to note this:
It is possible that only by repeated and costly failure, such as the Manitoba Government telephones, will the public realize that the proper function of Government is not the conduct of industries but the impartial inspection of them under intelligent laws, adapted to the character and conditions of the community and the country.
Another authority in this matter is Mr. Acworth himself, who says that we can expect higher rates under nationalization than under the company system. In his book "The Railway and the Trader," Mr. Acworth supports Professor Hadley in saying:
It is a mistake to expect lower rates or better facilities from Government than from private companies. The actual results are just the reverse. The State is more apt to tax industry than to foster it; and when it attempts to tax industry, it is even less responsible than a private company. State management is more costly than private management, thus much capital is wasted. State management is demoralizing, both to legitimate business and politics.
This is the generally accepted view of economists. It was the view of statesmen up to 1896 who always preferred private ownership operation to government ownership. We may say that the Bill which is before the House is for the purpose of buying outright the Grand Trunk railway system. To me it seems the greatest and most complicated undertaking that has ever been urged on such weak grounds. The railway has a length of about 4,000 miles, its tracks measuring about 6,300 miles. It extends into the United States, >to Chicago in the west, and Portland in the east. The capital invested is about $420,000,000.	.
One of the reasons advanced by the Hydiro-Electric Commission for this deal is that it would be in the interests of a
74}
great number of municipalities who are responsible for the operation of the HydroElectric system. Another argument advanced in favour of the Bill is that it would give the Canadian Northern railway, already under Government control, terminal facilities which otherwise the Government would have to build or.acquire. The sponsors of the Bill claim that the Grand Trunk will also serve as a feeder to the National railways in the West.
In order to attain the object of this Bill the Government will have to raise more money on the credit of the people of Canada, whose burdens have already reached nearly the limit. In my humble opinion, not a cent more can be added to their burdens without causing great danger, if not disaster, to the country. We find that in recent years nearly $367,000,000, or one-third of our national debt has been ' spent on our railways, while the operation of these roads by the Government has produced a deficit of about $13,000,000. Not a cent of interest on capital expenditure has ever been earned by these government roads. Calculating at the rate of 4 per cent we find that the interest on capital expenditure on government railways no<w approximates $15,000,000 annually, and that it grows from year to year. That to my mind is not very reassuring.
All these questions of terminal facilities and feeders for the Government system can be solved by making arrangements for interchange of traffic between the Government system and the Grand Trunk. The Grand Trunk railway in central Canada may be made a feeder to the National Transcontinental, and the latter a feeder to the Grand Trunk railway. The Grand Trunk terminals can be made available to the Government roads. By these easy business methods the taxpayers can be relieved of assuming this great new obligation. The whole people of this country have their eyes on Ottawa. They are begging and clamouring the Government not to consummate this gigantic deal. We can gauge the feeling of the country at large by the views of the press. The Gazette said recently:
It is the worst news that has come to us since the war. This means that the Grand Trunk railway will be undermined and put on the same level as the Intercolonial railway.
There is no doubt that the operation of a new line of railway by the Government would largely increase1 our national debt and create additional deficits which the country will ultimately have to pay. In
